newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM sticks to his economic guns, so far.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM sticks to his economic guns, so far.

text.p: Prime Minister Costas Simitis appears determined to get his message across to unruly farmers and state workers: Greeks must sacrifice more to ensure they join a planned single European currency.
"Demands for billions of drachmas cannot be satisfied. To do so would be a step backward," Simitis, a frosty pro-European technocrat, told the nation. "The state has no more to give."
He has refused to yield to demands for cash in a three-week showdown with farmers, who have blocked national roads and caused more than $100 million in damage to the economy.
Simitis and National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou have shown no hint of weakening and appear determined to face down disgruntled farmers and workers early in their term.
"The position of the government is clear. We shall not give in," Papandoniou said this week. "The government is really very, very worried about the situation. Our patience is wearing thin."
Simitis and Papandoniou have said "no" so many times to farmers' demands for such things as cheaper fuel and higher subsidies that the credibility of the socialist government is on the line.
"Simitis is not willing to give in because that would mean forfeiting his economic programme," said Thanos Veremis, head of the Hellenic Foundation for European and Foreign Policy.
The government fears that yielding to the farmers would open a Pandora's box, with unions piling in with their own demands.
Despite a sharp fall in his popularity ratings, Simitis has stuck to a "business as usual" approach throughout the farmers' blockade and accompanying union protests around the country.

With a deadpan, professorial style, he has done little to reassure teachers, doctors, seamen, civil servants, dockers and diplomats who have gone on strike in recent weeks to protest against his measures.
"He is not good at public relations, that's for sure," said Veremis. "He lacks personnel charisma which might help people accept what he is trying to do."
But his message has remained steadfast. Greece will join European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 2001 -- with its single currency -- and Greeks will bear any burden to get there.

To that end he has imposed numerous new taxes, abolished many exemptions and gone after Greece's legion of tax evaders. He will hire one new civil servant for every five who retire, near heresy in a land where political patronage is king.
The self-avowed socialist reformer often sounds more like a neo-conservative economist. He called and won early elections in September, giving him a four-year mandate to impose his reforms.
"He's doing what we thought he would do, acting early in his term to get the bad news behind him," one EU diplomat said.

Those quick moves have damaged Simitis's popularity, with his rating falling to 37.9 percent from 49.7 percent last June. Even harsher was the view of 75.8 percent of those questioned that his economic measures have been unfair.
But Simitis's appears to have fixed his sights on joining EMU with a second group of EU states by 2001 and he has been unmoved by warnings of possible fallout on the social front.
That may be because he controls 163 seats in the 300-seat parliament with no hints of defections among socialist deputies and no opposition capable of exploiting the situation.
The conservative New Democracy party is split and without any charismatic leader to challenge Simitis's policies.
